title: Making fresh sausages at home
subtitle: A basic recipe and method for natural-cased pork sausages.
excerpt: Home-made sausages from your own pork need only a mincer or food processor, a sausage stuffer, natural casings, and a simple seasoning. They contain no preservatives or fillers and keep for three days refrigerated or three months frozen. Here is the method for approximately 1 kg of pork sausages.
sourceNotes: Jane Grigson, Charcuterie and French Pork Cookery (1967). River Cottage Meat Book (Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall, 2004). Guild of Q Butchers, sausage making guidance.

glossaryTerms.definition: The cleaned, salted intestine of a pig, sheep, or ox used as a casing for sausages. Pork sausages typically use hog casings (from the pig's small intestine), which are sold in salt by weight.

The cohesion of fat and meat in a sausage mix. Proper bind depends on keeping the meat cold throughout mixing, so that the myosin proteins in the meat stay intact and entrap the fat. Warm meat fat causes the sausage to cook greasy.

content.text: A well-made sausage depends on cold meat, a correct fat-to-lean ratio, and good
. The standard fat ratio for a juicy, flavourful sausage is 20 to 25% fat to total meat weight. Below 15% the sausage is dry and crumbly; above 30% it is greasy.
250 g pork back fat (if shoulder is lean)
5 g white pepper, 2 g dried sage, 1 g ground mace
: approximately 1.5 m, soaked in cold water for 30 minutes, rinsed through with water
Keep all equipment and meat cold throughout. Chill the mincer parts in the freezer for 30 minutes before starting. The meat should be just above freezing, not room temperature.
Cut the pork into 3 cm cubes and mince through a medium (6 mm) plate.

Mix the salt and seasonings into the cold mince, adding the ice water as you mix. Mix vigorously by hand for 2 to 3 minutes until the mixture becomes slightly sticky. This is the protein bind developing.
Cook a small patty of the mix in a dry pan and taste for seasoning. Adjust before stuffing.

Thread a length of soaked casing onto the sausage stuffer tube. Fill the stuffer barrel with the sausage mix. Ease the casing off the tube as the mix fills it, keeping the fill firm but not so tight the casing bursts. Leave 5 cm of empty casing at each end.
Twist the filled rope into sausages by pinching and twisting alternate portions clockwise and anticlockwise. Standard sausages are approximately 10 cm long.
Refrigerate uncovered for one hour to allow the casing to dry slightly and firm up before cooking or freezing.
